edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De baptismo, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Exinde, egressi de lavacro, perungimur benedicta unctione de pristina disciplina, qua ungi oleo de cornu in sacerdotium solebant. Ex quo Aaron a Moyse unctus est: unde Christus dicitur, a chrismate quod est unctio, quae Domino nomen accommodavit, facta spiritualis, quia spiritu unctus est a Deo Patre, sicut in Actis: Collecti sunt enim vere in ista civitate adversus sanctum Filium tuum, quem unxisti. Sic et in nobis carnaliter currit unctio, sed spiritaliter proficit: quomodo et ipsius Baptismi carnalis actus, quod in aqua mergimur; spiritalis effectus, quod delictis liberamur.
pass_a_gloss: From there, having gone out from the bath, we are anointed with blessed anointing from the former discipline, by which they used to anoint with oil from the horn into the priesthood. From which Aaron was anointed by Moses: whence Christ is called, from the chrism which is anointing, which accommodated the name to the Lord, made spiritual, because He was anointed with the Spirit by God the Father, as in the Acts: For they were gathered together in this city against Your holy Son, whom You anointed. So also in us the anointing runs carnally, but profits spiritually: just as also the bodily act of that very Baptism, which is that we are immersed in water; the spiritual effect, which is that we are freed from sins.

choices.why: chrism refers to the anointing oil

bible_refs.note: Collecti sunt enim vere in ista civitate adversus sanctum Filium tuum, quem unxisti

pass_b_english: Afterward, we step from the bath and are anointed with blessed oil, following the ancient rite by which priests were anointed with oil from a horn. This goes back to Aaron, whom Moses anointed. From that practice comes the very name ‘Christ,’ from ‘chrism’ meaning anointing—a title that fitted the Lord because He was made spiritual, anointed with the Spirit by God the Father, just as Acts says: ‘They were gathered together in this city against Your holy Son, whom You anointed’ (Acts 4:27). In the same way, the anointing runs on our bodies but works in our spirits, just as Baptism itself is a bodily act—we are plunged in water—whose spiritual effect is that we are freed from sins.

anf_compare.notes: Drafted from source only; ANF not shown to drafter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies the scripture reference (Acts 4:27) which was alluded to in the Latin 'sicut in Actis: Collecti sunt enim vere in ista civitate adversus sanctum Filium tuum, quem unxisti'. Pass A and B are consistent with the source's meaning regarding the distinction between the carnal act and spiritual effect.
